chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Abu Ubaydah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man from us who buys from the ruler from the camels and sheep of the zakat, while he knows that they take from them more than the right that is obligatory upon them. He said, so he said: 'The camels and sheep are no different than wheat and barley and other than that; there is no harm with it until you recognize the forbidden (part) with your own eye.'

It was said to him: 'And what do you think regarding a zakat collector who comes to us and takes the zakat of our sheep, so we say to him: Sell them, and he sells them to us; what do you say regarding their purchase from him?' He said: 'If he has taken them and separated them, then there is no harm.'

It was said to him: 'And what do you think regarding the purchase of wheat and barley? The distributor comes to us, divides our share and takes his share, and sets it aside by measure. What do you think regarding the purchase of that food from him?' He said: 'If he has taken it by measure, and you are present at that, then there is no harm in purchasing it from him without measure.'
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to buy zakat goods from the government or collectors who may have taken extra?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the principle of *istishab al-hal* (presumption of continuity) in commercial transactions, ruling that zakat assets remain permissible for purchase even if the collector is known to have over-extracted, unless the specific forbidden portion is distinctly identified. This ruling extends to grain distributed by volume, allowing buyers to purchase it by weight or count without re-measurement, provided the initial separation occurred in their presence. This highlights the Shia juristic preference for ease in trade (*sahh al-mu'amalat*) and the distinction between general impurity of collection and specific identifiable haram.
